source: Kalyuga (2007) Expertise reversal effect and its implications for learner-tailored instruction
finding: Definition: methods that help low-knowledge learners lose value, or hurt, for higher-knowledge learners. Seen as a redundancy effect: guidance becomes redundant against the learner's own stored knowledge.
numbers: Review covers about 40 studies; Table 1 gives novice and expert effect sizes for each.
quote: Instructional formats, techniques, and procedures that are optimal for novices may hinder relative performance of learners who are more experienced
limits: Narrow definition of expertise: skill on one task class, not general expertise. Most studies are cross-sectional, with groups split by a pretest.
agent_relevance: Guidance must be tied to the agent's skill on one task class, not to the agent overall.

source: Kalyuga (2007) Expertise reversal effect and its implications for learner-tailored instruction
finding: Theory: knowledge in long-term memory plays an executive role. Novices need outside guidance as a substitute. Experts have the knowledge, so outside guidance must be reconciled with it and adds extraneous load.
numbers: Mid-level learners: both sources are complementary. Guidance should cover the unfamiliar parts only.
limits: This is a verbal theory. It gives no formula for the crossover point.
agent_relevance: Show a lesson only for the unfamiliar part of a task class, not for all of it. This is the S0 design rule.

source: Kalyuga, Chandler and Sweller (1998) Levels of expertise and instructional design, as tabulated in Kalyuga 2007
finding: Founding longitudinal study. Electrical trainees saw wiring diagrams with embedded text vs diagram only. Embedded text won for novices. After intensive training, diagram only won.
numbers: Operation and troubleshooting test: d = 1.67 novices (N=17), -0.44 experts (N=30), difference 2.11. Fault-finding test: d = 1.89 novices, -0.88 experts, difference 2.77.
limits: Read only through the 2007 review table, not the original paper. The same trainees were tested as skill grew.
agent_relevance: Strongest single reversal. The same material flips sign within one learner population as skill grows, so a static prompt cannot be right for the whole run.

source: Kalyuga, Chandler and Sweller (2000) animated diagram with narration vs diagram only, as tabulated in Kalyuga 2007
finding: Mechanical engineering trainees. Narrated explanation with animated diagram helped novices. After several training sessions, the diagram-only group beat the narrated group.
numbers: d = 1.18 novices (N=30), -0.62 experts (N=38), difference 1.80.
limits: Via review table only.
agent_relevance: Commentary on something the learner already understands costs attention.

source: Kalyuga, Chandler, Tuovinen and Sweller (2001) Learner experience and efficiency of instructional guidance, as tabulated in Kalyuga 2007
finding: Worked examples beat problem solving for novices when programming relay circuits. The edge vanished with training. In a second experiment on switching equations there was no difference at first, then problem solving won after training.
numbers: Exp 1 relay programs: d = 0.90 novices (N=24), 0.23 experts (N=24), diff 0.67. Exp 2 switching equations: d = -0.26 novices (N=24), -0.75 experts (N=24), diff 0.49.
limits: In Exp 2 novices showed no clear benefit; the reversal is only at the late stage. Via review table only.
agent_relevance: Example benefit can fade to zero then negative on the same task class.

source: Kalyuga et al. (2001a) worked examples vs exploratory learning, Exp 2, as tabulated in Kalyuga 2007
finding: Full disordinal interaction. Worked examples first beat exploratory learning, then exploratory learning won as expertise grew.
numbers: d = 0.69 novices (N=17), -0.33 experts (N=17), difference 1.02.
limits: Small samples. Via review table only.
agent_relevance: Free exploration is the right mode only after a base of knowledge exists.

source: Kalyuga and Sweller (2004) Exp 3, coordinate geometry, as described in Kalyuga 2007
finding: High-school students were split by median on a rapid pretest, then randomly given worked examples or problem solving. Less knowledgeable learners gained more from worked examples. More knowledgeable learners showed a problem-solving benefit. The interaction was significant.
numbers: d = 1.20 novices (N=21), -0.36 experts (N=21), difference 1.56. He-Yueya 2024 adds that the original had 42 Year 9 students and 8 practice problems, with worked solutions for the odd-numbered ones.
limits: A median split on a pretest creates groups prone to regression. The expert-side effect is not individually significant.
agent_relevance: Template for a test in our setting: split by pass rate on the task class, randomise lesson on or off, compare.

source: Tuovinen and Sweller (1999), as tabulated in Kalyuga 2007
finding: Database program learning. Worked examples beat exploration for novices. For higher-knowledge students there was no difference.
numbers: d = 0.91 novices (N=17), -0.31 experts (N=15), difference 1.22.
limits: The expert-side reversal is not reliable.
agent_relevance: Many reversals are really a disappearance of benefit. Dropping the lesson for strong classes is safe even where it is not better.

source: Reisslein, Atkinson, Seeling and Reisslein (2006) example-problem vs problem-example vs faded, as tabulated in Kalyuga 2007
finding: Engineering students learning circuit analysis. Novices benefited from example-then-problem pairs. Experts benefited from problem-then-example pairs and from faded sequences.
numbers: Example-problem vs problem-example: d = 0.33 novices (N=62), -0.37 experts (N=60). Example-problem vs faded: d = 0.28 (N=63) vs -0.26 (N=61).
limits: Effects are small and groups are about 60 each.
agent_relevance: Order matters. For a strong class, attempt first and show a solution only after a miss.

source: Reisslein (2005) dissertation, pace of fading, as described in Kalyuga 2007
finding: The pace of moving from examples to problems interacted with prior knowledge. High-knowledge learners did better with fast or immediate transition. Low-knowledge learners did better with slow transition.
numbers: Slow vs fast transition: d = 1.30 novices (N=39), -0.47 experts (N=44), difference 1.77. Fast fading = one step removed per example, slow = one step per two examples.
limits: Dissertation. Via review only.
agent_relevance: Fading rate can be set by competence. Fade faster when pass rate is high.

source: Lee, Plass and Homer (2006) iconic vs symbolic representations, as described in Kalyuga 2007
finding: Gas-law simulation. Added icons helped low-knowledge students and hurt high-knowledge students, but only when two parameters were shown at once. With all three parameters at once, icons helped everyone.
numbers: d = 0.30 novices (N=48), -1.39 experts (N=63), difference 2.99.
limits: The reversal disappears when task load is high for everyone.
agent_relevance: Boundary condition: support stays useful for everyone on very hard tasks.

source: Yeung, Jin and Sweller (1998) integrated vs glossary vocabulary, as described in Kalyuga 2007
finding: Fifth graders did better with in-text definitions. University students did better with a separate glossary. Experts reported lower load with the minimal format.
numbers: Expert d from -0.53 to -0.79 across experiments; differences 0.66 to 1.87.
limits: Age and expertise are confounded.
agent_relevance: Age is a weak proxy for skill. Use a measured class pass rate.

source: Salden, Paas and van Merrienboer (2006); Camp et al. (2001); Kalyuga and Sweller (2004, 2005), adaptive task selection, as described in Kalyuga 2007
finding: Tasks chosen by the learner's measured performance (and effort) beat non-adapted task sequences. Two ways of adapting (efficiency-based and learner preference) did not differ in air traffic control training.
numbers: Salden 2006 adapted vs non-adapted: effect size 0.58. Kalyuga and Sweller 2004: d = 0.46 knowledge gain. Kalyuga and Sweller 2005 (with load rating): d = 0.55 knowledge, 0.69 efficiency.
limits: Different adaptation rules performed equally, so the gain is from adapting at all.
agent_relevance: Supports a measured, code-run gate. The exact rule matters little; having one matters.

source: Kalyuga (2006, 2007) and Kalyuga and Sweller (2004, 2005) rapid assessment methods, as described in Kalyuga 2007
finding: Computational model of adaptation: a rapid first-step test or a rapid step-verification test places the learner on a guidance level. The learner moves to less guidance when the rapid test is passed and the load rating is low. The efficiency indicator is performance divided by rated load.
numbers: Correlation with full tests up to .92; test time cut by up to 4.9x (first-step). Verification test: r = .71 and .75 with observed solving, time cut 3.2x and 3.5x; sentence comprehension 3.7x.
limits: Validated on well-defined tasks (algebra, geometry, kinematics). Poorly defined tasks are harder.
agent_relevance: Blueprint for S0: a cheap probe of the class, then pick the guidance level. For an agent the probe is a few held-out items run by code.

source: Renkl, Atkinson and Maier (2000) From example study to problem solving: smooth transitions help learning (Research Report 140)
finding: Backward fading vs example-problem pairs. A field study with low-track students and a lab study with university students. Fading improved near transfer. Far transfer did not improve.
numbers: Field study: near transfer F(1,32)=4.44, p<.05; far transfer F(1,32)=2.28, p>.10. Lab study N=54 (27 per group): near transfer F(1,51)=4.58, p<.05; far transfer F<1; errors during learning F(1,51)=7.62, p<.05. Reliability alpha .85 near, .60 far (field).
quote: this effect is mediated by a lower number of errors under the fading condition
limits: The 2000 report precedes the published versions. Mean tables in the PDF text are garbled. Far transfer was null both times.
agent_relevance: Fading removes the cliff between a full example and a bare problem and reduces errors during learning. Fading alone does not give transfer to new structures.

source: Atkinson, Renkl and Merrill (2003) Transitioning from studying examples to solving problems
finding: Fading alone helps near transfer but not reliably far transfer. Adding prompts to name the principle behind each step gave medium to large effects on both, with no extra time.
numbers: Two experiments; the abstract reports medium to large effects on near and far transfer and no added learning time.
limits: Only the abstract was read this session. Exact N and effect values were not captured.
agent_relevance: A fade is stronger if each remaining step also asks the learner to name its rule. In an agent: ask for the rule when a step is removed.

source: Nievelstein, van Gog, van Dijck and Boshuizen (2013) Worked example and expertise reversal in less structured tasks: legal case reasoning
finding: Failed to find a reversal. First-year and third-year law students both did better with worked examples than with problem solving, although third-year students had far more prior knowledge.
numbers: First-year N about 75 (cells 19/19/19/18): test score 58.63 (SD 27.74) with examples vs 8.59 (SD 4.06) with problem solving, F(1,68)=105.2, f=1.24. Third-year N=36 (9 per cell): 82.28 (SD 18.11) vs 37.06 (SD 26.71), F(1,32)=37.03, f=1.02. Prior knowledge: third-year 17.12 vs first-year 8.86, d = 2.75. Learning time: examples about 570 s vs 1146 s for problem solving (first-year).
limits: Authors argue less structured tasks take longer to master, so advanced students are still novices at the schema level. Process-step prompts had a small effect for first-years only.
agent_relevance: Boundary condition. If the task class is open ended, examples stay useful even for a strong model. Expertise is task-specific, not global.

source: Rourke and Sweller (2009), as described in Chen (2016) thesis
finding: Art history students identifying a designer's style. Worked examples beat problem solving for both first-year and second-year students. No expertise reversal.
numbers: No numbers captured.
limits: Reported in the thesis review chapter only. Second-year students may still lack the key knowledge.
agent_relevance: Another null in an ill-structured domain.

source: Kyun, Kalyuga and Sweller (2013) English literature, as described in Chen (2016) thesis
finding: Three experiments with falling prior knowledge. The worked example advantage appeared gradually as knowledge dropped: none for the most expert, retention only for the middle, retention plus marginal transfer for the least.
numbers: No numbers captured.
limits: Reported in the thesis review chapter only.
agent_relevance: Shows a graded dose-response, not a sharp switch.

source: Chen (2016) The worked example effect, the generation effect and element interactivity (PhD thesis, UNSW), Experiments 1-3
finding: Geometry. Grade 4 novices: worked examples beat problem solving on high-interactivity items, and generating beat being shown on low-interactivity items. Grade 6: both effects smaller. Grade 7 (revision of last year's topic): the worked-example effect reversed and low guidance won on both item types.
numbers: Exp 1: 41 Grade 4 students recruited, 33 analysed. Generation effect Cohen d = .96 (Exp 1) and .57 (Exp 2, 1-tailed). Exp 3 (Grade 7): interaction gone, worked example effect reversed.
limits: Short sessions, immediate tests. The journal paper is Chen, Kalyuga and Sweller (2017).
agent_relevance: Expertise lowers element interactivity. Whether a lesson helps depends on how many interacting pieces the item still has for this agent, not on the topic label.

source: Chen (2016) thesis, Experiments 4-5, trigonometry with delayed tests
finding: Exp 4: no interaction on an immediate test. On a test a week later the interaction appeared: examples helped on high-interactivity items, generating helped on low-interactivity items. Exp 5 (more knowledgeable students): more guidance hurt on both item types, on immediate and delayed tests.
numbers: Exp 4 immediate: no significant interaction. Exp 4 delayed: significant guidance by interactivity interaction. Exp 5: generation effect on both tests, no worked example effect.
limits: The immediate test failed to show the effect; only the delayed test did. The author notes the worked example effect has rarely been tested with delayed tests.
agent_relevance: Measure retention after a delay, not just the immediate pass. An agent run has no delay unless we build one (new session, new item set).

source: Chen, Kalyuga and Sweller (2017) The expertise reversal effect is a variant of the more general element interactivity effect
finding: Theory move: expertise reversal is a special case of the element interactivity effect. Expertise folds interacting elements into one schema, so item complexity falls and guidance becomes redundant.
numbers: Cited 200 times per OpenAlex (checked this session). Abstract not retrievable; content taken from the thesis summary.
limits: Not opened. The paper is paywalled.
agent_relevance: Predicts which items still need lessons: those with many interacting elements for this model.

source: Leppink, Broers, Imbos, van der Vleuten and Berger (2011) Self-explanation in the domain of statistics: an expertise reversal effect
finding: First-year statistics students. For conceptual understanding there was a crossover. Low prior knowledge students learned most from worked examples. High prior knowledge students learned most from writing arguments, and open-ended questions alone were worst.
numbers: Interaction F(3,97)=2.762, p<.05, eta2=.079. Low prior: worked examples best vs questions plus arguments worst, t(25)=2.415, d=0.96. High prior: arguments best vs questions only worst, t(25)=2.688, d=1.06; examples vs arguments d=0.51, not significant. One-way effects not significant (eta2 .122 and .114). About 130 students recruited, about 105 analysed.
limits: Underpowered. The main interaction is only just significant. No interaction for propositional knowledge.
agent_relevance: A real crossover on understanding, not on recall. Lessons may matter for reasoning more than for facts.

source: Rey and Buchwald (2011) The expertise reversal effect: cognitive load and motivational explanations
finding: Replicated the reversal for the redundancy principle (text added to animation). Cognitive load differences, not motivation, explained it.
numbers: N = 104 students; 2 (novice or expert-trained) x 2 (extra text or not) design; gradient descent topic; about 30 minutes. Novices with extra text scored higher on retention and transfer; experts the reverse.
limits: Abstract only. Experts were created by a short earlier training, not years of skill.
agent_relevance: Short training can create the effect, so even a brief prior exposure to the task class may flip the sign.

source: Tetzlaff, Simonsmeier, Peters and Brod (2025) A cornerstone of adaptivity: a meta-analysis of the expertise reversal effect
finding: First large meta-analysis. Low prior knowledge learners do better with high assistance. High prior knowledge learners do better with low assistance. The effect is asymmetric.
numbers: 1590 studies screened, 60 studies, 176 effect sizes, 5924 participants. d = 0.505 for low prior knowledge (high assistance better). d = -0.428 for high prior knowledge (low assistance better).
limits: Moderators: type of prior-knowledge test, educational level, domain. Weaker for younger students, humanities and language learning. Only the abstract was read (via OpenAlex); full text not retrieved.
agent_relevance: Best current estimate: help on weak classes is worth about half a standard deviation; withholding help on strong classes gains slightly less. Do not expect large gains from removing lessons.

source: Grosse (2015) Fostering modeling competencies: benefits of worked examples, problems to be solved, and fading procedures
finding: Eighth graders. Fading did not beat example-problem pairs overall. Example-problem pairs were best for translating a real situation to maths. Backward fading was best only for intra-mathematical skills.
numbers: N=143; forward fading 37, backward fading 35, example-problem 35, problem-example 36. Translation: condition F(3,138)=2.93, p=.036, partial eta2=.060; with vs without fading F(1,138)=2.34, p=.129. Example-problem vs problem-example p=.015. Modelling score: condition F(3,138)=.20, p=.897. Prior knowledge was the strongest predictor (partial eta2 .126 to .150).
limits: No pure-problem control. Groups were not split by prior knowledge, so the reversal prediction was not tested. Corresponding-author surname used for the citation.
agent_relevance: Failed-replication signal for fading: no general edge over example-then-problem. The fade direction and the skill being taught change the result.

source: Retnowati (2017) Faded-example as a tool to acquire and automate mathematics knowledge
finding: Frames the faded example as the right format for learners who know some of the material but still need practice to automate it. Full examples add load for advanced learners and bare problems load novices.
numbers: No new data. Conceptual review for trigonometry.
limits: Narrative review in a conference paper. No effect sizes.
agent_relevance: Fade fits the middle of the skill range. Three zones: full example, faded, bare problem.

source: He-Yueya, Goodman and Brunskill (2024) Evaluating and optimizing educational content with large language model judgments
finding: GPT-3.5 acting as a simulated expert predicted post-test scores for 120 student personas. It reproduced the pattern of the Kalyuga and Sweller experiment: worked examples helped low-skill personas and made no difference for high-skill personas.
numbers: 120 personas, skill levels 1 to 5 on two skills, split at the median. 8 algebra word problems, worked solutions for 4. gpt-3.5-turbo-16k, temperature 0.
limits: This is an LLM's belief about students, not human data. It reproduced the ordinal pattern (no difference), not a true reversal. The model may have seen the original studies.
agent_relevance: The model knows the expertise reversal pattern when asked about students. That says nothing about how the model behaves as a learner.

source: Xu and Wu (2026) Skill availability and presentation granularity in LLM agents: a controlled SkillsBench study
finding: Agents with a skill document beat agents without one. Adding one worked example to medium-level guidance changed little.
numbers: 30 tasks, 5 trials each, 1800 rows. GPT-5.5: no skill 31.3%, medium no example 61.3%, medium with example 62.0%. DeepSeek V4-Flash: no skill 26.0%, medium no example 44.0%, with example 45.3%. Example effect +0.7 and +1.3 points, CI crossed zero. Detectable difference about 8 to 16 points.
limits: Tasks were not split by model competence, so the reversal prediction was not tested. Underpowered for small effects.
agent_relevance: Direct measure on agents: a worked example inside a skill adds near zero on average. The average may hide a crossover by task class. Test with a per-class split.

source: Qiu et al. (2026) When correct demonstrations hurt: rethinking the role of exemplars in in-context learning
finding: Correct demonstrations can lower accuracy. The damage grows for smaller models, harder tasks and more perturbed demonstrations. Larger models were stable.
numbers: LLaMA-2-7B fell from 96.4% to 56.9% from 0% to 100% perturbation. LLaMA-3.1-8B fell from 98.2% to 66.0%. Larger models stayed within about 2% of clean accuracy.
limits: Perturbations are input changes that keep the answer correct. Not the same as knowledge-redundant examples. Not a test of expertise reversal.
agent_relevance: Indirect evidence that the exemplar effect depends on model capability. Strong models are less moved by examples.
